application: Upper-air weather observation radiosondes. Balloon-borne transmitters sending temperature, humidity, pressure, wind data during ascent.
typical_devices: Vaisala RS41-SG/SGP (tunable 400.16-405.99 MHz, ~60 mW TX power, GFSK modulation, 4.8 kHz peak deviation), Graw DFM-17 (GNSS radiosonde, ~100 mW TX, continuous frequency selection)
regulatory_ref: ITU RR Article 5, footnote 5.282; WMO CIMO Guide
notes: Radiosondes are expendable; over 800,000 synoptic flights per year worldwide. Frequency selected per launch to avoid co-channel interference with nearby stations. RS41 has replaced the older RS92 in most national weather services.

service: Meteorological Satellite (Earth-to-space), Space Operation, Earth Exploration-Satellite
application: Data Collection Platforms (DCP) uplink to geostationary meteorological satellites. Environmental monitoring buoys, river gauges, seismic sensors transmit telemetry.
typical_devices: NOAA GOES DCS uplink transmitters (10 W into wide-beam antenna, relayed via L-band ~1680 MHz), EUMETSAT Meteosat DCP receivers, Sutron XLite/SatLink3 data loggers
power_limit: Typically 10 W EIRP for DCP transmitters
regulatory_ref: ITU RR 5.208B; NOAA GOES DCS channel plan; WMO Manual on GOS
notes: GOES DCS channels span 401.7-402.4 MHz. International DCS (IDCS) channels spaced 3 kHz apart from 402.0355-402.0655 MHz. Channels I23-I33 (402.0685-402.0985 MHz) allocated to EUMETSAT for regional use. Government primary use for meteorological satellite and earth exploration satellite (Earth-to-space only).

application: Ultra-low-power wireless communication between implanted medical devices and external programmer/monitor units. Range 2-5 meters. Used for pacemaker interrogation, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) data retrieval, neurostimulator programming.
typical_devices: Medtronic Micra leadless pacemaker (Bluetooth LE + MICS telemetry), Abbott Assurity MRI pacemaker (RF telemetry), Biotronik Edora 8 pacemaker (wandless MICS telemetry for home monitoring), Boston Scientific ACCOLADE MRI pacemaker (ZIP telemetry)
regulatory_ref: ITU-R SA.1346; ETSI EN 301 839 (EU); FCC 47 CFR Part 95 Subpart I (US, MedRadio); ECC/REC/(02)01
notes: 10 channels of 300 kHz each within the 402-405 MHz core band. Frequency error shall not exceed +/-100 ppm. Wing bands at 401-402 MHz and 405-406 MHz added by FCC in 2009 (MedRadio expansion). MICS is ITU worldwide allocation ensuring interoperability for patients traveling internationally. Biotronik and Medtronic developed home monitoring systems using MICS band.

application: Medical implant telemetry per ETSI EN 301 839
typical_devices: Medtronic Micra, Abbott Assurity MRI, Biotronik Edora 8, Boston Scientific ACCOLADE
regulatory_ref: ETSI EN 301 839; ANFR TNRBF; ECC/DEC/(01)17
notes: Harmonized across EU per ECC Decision. ANFR manages national implementation. Same technical parameters as worldwide ITU allocation.

application: Medical implant communications, body-worn medical devices, medical body area networks (MBAN)
typical_devices: Medtronic Micra, Abbott Assurity MRI, Boston Scientific ACCOLADE, Biotronik Edora 8
regulatory_ref: FCC 47 CFR Part 95 Subpart I; FCC 09-23 (MedRadio R&O)
notes: FCC expanded MICS to MedRadio in 2009, adding wing bands 401-402 MHz and 405-406 MHz for medical body area networks. Core band 402-405 MHz unchanged at 25 uW EIRP, 300 kHz channels.

application: Radiosonde transmissions for upper-air weather observation. Primary band for radiosonde operations in many countries.
typical_devices: Vaisala RS41-SG (tunable across 400.16-405.99 MHz), Graw DFM-17 (commonly set to 403 MHz area), Meteomodem M10/M20, InterMet iMet-4
regulatory_ref: ITU RR Article 5; ITU-R RS.1165
notes: 403-406 MHz is the most heavily used portion for radiosonde systems globally. Almost all national meteorological services operate radiosondes in this sub-band. Co-channel sharing with other services assessed as generally not feasible except under strict conditions.

application: Emergency distress alerting via satellite. EPIRB (maritime), PLB (personal/land), ELT (aviation). Internationally protected frequency - transmissions restricted exclusively to distress signaling.
typical_devices: ACR GlobalFix V4 EPIRB (406 MHz + 121.5 MHz homing, 66-ch GPS, 5W output), McMurdo SmartFind G8 AIS EPIRB (406 MHz + AIS), Ocean Signal rescueME PLB3 (406 MHz PLB, 66-ch GPS), Kannad SafeLink Solo PLB, ACR ResQLink 400 PLB
modulation: Phase modulation (PM), digital message encoding per C/S T.001
power_limit: 5 W (+37 dBm) typical EPIRB/PLB output power
regulatory_ref: ITU RR 5.267; ITU-R M.633; ETSI EN 300 066; Cospas-Sarsat C/S T.001 (beacon specs), C/S T.012 (channel plan); IMO SOLAS Chapter IV; ICAO Annex 10, ITU RR footnote 5.266 (no harmful interference)
notes: ABSOLUTELY PROTECTED BAND worldwide. No other transmissions permitted. Channel plan per C/S T.012 covers 406.025-406.076 MHz with channels at 406.025, 406.028, 406.031, 406.037, 406.040 MHz and more. Beacons transmit 0.5s burst every 50s. LEOSAR (Cospas) and GEOSAR (GOES/Meteosat/INSAT) satellite detection. MEOSAR (Galileo/GLONASS/GPS SAR) provides near-instantaneous global coverage with return link service. All 406 MHz beacons must be registered with national authority. [FACTCHECK ADDITION: ITU RR 5.266 also applies — prohibits harmful interference to Cospas-Sarsat band.]

service: Radio Astronomy, Fixed, Mobile, Space Research
application: Radio astronomy observations, land mobile communications, fixed links. Shared allocation varies by ITU region.
typical_devices: Radio telescope receivers (continuum observations), land mobile radio base stations
modulation: Various (FM for mobile, passive receive for radio astronomy)
regulatory_ref: ITU RR Article 5; ITU-R RA.769 (radio astronomy protection criteria)
notes: Radio astronomy has protection requirements per ITU-R RA.769. Mobile and fixed services share on condition of not causing harmful interference to radio astronomy. 406.1-410 MHz is a transition zone between protected 406 MHz distress band and land mobile allocations.

application: SNCF railway analogue radio (legacy), PMR professional mobile radio networks, military systems
typical_devices: Motorola DP4800 (403-470 MHz UHF, DMR, 4W, 1000 channels), SNCF train-to-ground radio equipment, Hytera PD785 DMR portable
power_limit: Up to 25 W mobile, 50 W base station (licensed PMR)
regulatory_ref: ANFR TNRBF; ARCEP frequency authorization
notes: In France, 410-420 MHz includes SNCF legacy railway radio allocations and professional mobile radio. SNCF has been transitioning to GSM-R (900 MHz) and FRMCS but legacy 400 MHz equipment still in use on some lines. Military also uses portions of this band.

application: BOS Digitalfunk (TETRA-based emergency services digital radio), legacy analog BOS remnants, PMR
typical_devices: Motorola MTP6650 TETRA, Sepura SC21 TETRA, legacy BOS analog Motorola GM360
power_limit: Up to 30 W (TETRA base stations), 3 W (TETRA handheld)
regulatory_ref: BNetzA Frequenzplan; BOS-Funkrichtlinie
notes: Germany's BOS Digitalfunk (emergency services radio) operates on TETRA in the 380-400 MHz range primarily, but 410-420 MHz contains some BOS analog remnants and government/military allocations. BNetzA manages spectrum for non-federal, BDBOS for BOS network.

application: US Federal government exclusive use. Military, federal law enforcement, other government agencies.
typical_devices: Various federal government radio systems (classified/restricted information)
regulatory_ref: NTIA Manual of Regulations and Procedures for Federal Radio Frequency Management; 47 USC 305
notes: 410-420 MHz is allocated exclusively to US Federal government use, managed by NTIA (not FCC). Non-federal users cannot operate in this band. Includes Department of Defense, Department of Justice, and other federal agencies.

application: Ministry of Defence (primary user), some PMR and government communications
typical_devices: Military tactical radio systems, Bowman radio (legacy)
regulatory_ref: Ofcom UKFAT; UK Spectrum Strategy
notes: The 400 MHz range in the UK has MoD as a significant primary user. Civil PMR users share on a managed basis. Ofcom has conducted strategic reviews of UHF spectrum at 420-470 MHz.

application: Government and military communications, fixed links
typical_devices: Military radio systems
regulatory_ref: GRFC (General Radio Frequency Centre) frequency allocation table
notes: Russia allocates 410-420 MHz primarily for government and military use. GRFC manages spectrum allocation under the Ministry of Digital Development, Communications and Mass Media.

application: Government and military communications, land mobile radio
typical_devices: Various government/military radio equipment
regulatory_ref: MIIT National Frequency Allocation Table (effective July 1, 2023); SRRC regulations
notes: China's MIIT manages spectrum via SRRC (State Radio Regulation of China). The 410-420 MHz range is primarily allocated to government and military services. MIIT revised radio frequency allocations with latest version effective July 1, 2023.

application: Amateur radio (70cm band lower segment), military radiolocation (radar). Amateur stations must not cause interference to, and must accept interference from, government radiolocation.
typical_devices: Yaesu FT-70DR (amateur handheld, 144/430 MHz dual-band), Icom IC-9700 (amateur all-mode), military radar systems
modulation: FM, SSB, CW, digital modes (DMR, D-STAR, System Fusion)
power_limit: 1500 W PEP (amateur, FCC Part 97); military radiolocation varies
regulatory_ref: FCC 47 CFR Part 97; 47 CFR 97.303(h)(1)
notes: US amateur allocation uniquely extends down to 420 MHz (not 430 MHz as in Region 1). Amateurs must accept interference from and not cause interference to government radiolocation within 80.5 km of Buffalo, Cleveland, and Detroit. 420-430 MHz is secondary to radiolocation in some areas.

application: Ministry of Defence primary user, radiolocation systems. NOT amateur radio (amateur starts at 430 MHz in UK).
typical_devices: Military radar and communication systems
regulatory_ref: Ofcom UKFAT; Ofcom Strategic Review of UHF Spectrum at 420-470 MHz
notes: In the UK, 420-430 MHz is NOT available for amateur radio. Amateur allocation begins at 430 MHz. MoD is the primary user of this band.

application: Amateur radio 70cm band (part of broader 420-450 MHz US amateur allocation). Repeaters, simplex, satellite, weak signal, ATV, digital modes.
typical_devices: Yaesu FT-70DR, Kenwood TH-D75A, Icom IC-905, AMSAT satellites (435-438 MHz uplink/downlink), various DMR/D-STAR/Fusion repeaters
modulation: FM, SSB, CW, ATV (DATV), DMR (4FSK TDMA), D-STAR (GMSK), C4FM (System Fusion)
regulatory_ref: FCC 47 CFR Part 97.301(a); 47 CFR 97.303
notes: US amateur allocation is 420-450 MHz (30 MHz wide), much wider than Region 1's 430-440 MHz (10 MHz). Shared with radiolocation on a co-primary basis. +/- 5 MHz repeater offset standard. 432.1 MHz is weak signal calling frequency. 435-438 MHz includes amateur satellite allocations. No ISM overlay at 433 MHz in the US.

application: Amateur radio 70cm band. Repeaters, simplex, satellite, ATV, data, weak signal.
typical_devices: Yaesu FT-991A, Icom IC-7100, Kenwood TM-D710GA, various GB3xx repeaters
modulation: FM, SSB, CW, ATV, DMR, D-STAR, C4FM
power_limit: 40 W (16 dBW) ERP Full/Intermediate license in 430-432 MHz; 400 W ERP in other segments (with restrictions)
regulatory_ref: Ofcom UKFAT; RSGB band plan; Ofcom Amateur Radio License terms
notes: Secondary to MoD (Ministry of Defence) which is the primary user. 431-432 MHz not available within 100 km radius of Charing Cross, London. Repeaters/beacons above 25 W ERP require MoD coordination via Notice of Variation. Standard repeater shift is +1.6 MHz (input 430-432 MHz, output 438-440 MHz).

application: Amateur radio 70cm band. Limited in some areas due to military primary allocation.
typical_devices: Yaesu FT-70DR, Icom IC-9700, DMR repeaters (F1ZBD network)
modulation: FM, SSB, CW, DMR, D-STAR, C4FM, ATV
power_limit: 120 W (class 1 license), lower for other classes
regulatory_ref: ANFR TNRBF; ARCEP Decision 2014-1263; Arrete du 21 septembre 2000 (amateur radio)
notes: Secondary allocation. French military has primary usage in some geographic areas, which may restrict amateur operations. The 435-438 MHz segment includes amateur satellite allocations. ISM band 433.05-434.79 MHz overlays amateur allocation - amateurs must accept ISM interference.

application: Amateur radio 70cm band. Shared with ISM (433.05-434.79 MHz) and radiolocation.
typical_devices: Yaesu FT-991A, Icom IC-9700, Kenwood TH-D75A, DARC repeater network (DB0xx)
modulation: FM, SSB, CW, DMR, D-STAR, C4FM, DATV
power_limit: 750 W PEP (Class A license), 75 W PEP (Class E license)
regulatory_ref: BNetzA Frequenzplan; AFuV (Amateurfunkverordnung); DARC band plan
notes: Secondary to radiolocation (primary). ISM band 433.05-434.79 MHz overlays - amateur stations must accept interference from ISM devices. 435-438 MHz reserved for amateur satellite operations only (no local communications). Maximum bandwidth 2 MHz for digital modes, 7 MHz for AM-ATV.

application: Amateur radio 70cm band with gaps. Fixed and mobile services are co-primary in 430-435 MHz and 438-440 MHz segments.
typical_devices: Yaesu FT-70DR, Icom IC-9700, ARI repeater network (IR/IQ prefix)
modulation: FM, SSB, CW, DMR, D-STAR, C4FM
regulatory_ref: MISE/MIMIT frequency plan; ITU RR footnote 5.271 (Italy); ARI band plan
notes: Italy has a UNIQUE allocation structure: 430-434 MHz (amateur), 434-435 MHz (NOT amateur - reserved for other services), 435-438 MHz (amateur). The 1 MHz gap at 434-435 MHz is a significant restriction not found in most other European countries. Fixed service allocated on primary basis across 430-440 MHz per ITU footnote for Italy.

application: Amateur radio 70cm band. Repeaters, simplex, digital modes.
typical_devices: Yaesu FT-70DR, Icom IC-9700, EA/EB prefix repeaters
modulation: FM, SSB, CW, DMR, D-STAR, C4FM
power_limit: 50 W maximum transmitted power (200 W peak per CNAF)
regulatory_ref: CNAF (Cuadro Nacional de Atribucion de Frecuencias); BOE resolution; FEDI-EA band plan
notes: Spain allocates 430-440 MHz to amateur radio as secondary service. Maximum transmitted power 50 W with 200 W peak, 25 kHz bandwidth limit. Spain recently opened the 40 MHz (8m) band for amateurs (2024), showing progressive spectrum policy.

application: Amateur radio 70cm band. Shared with ISM (433.05-434.79 MHz) and fixed/mobile services.
typical_devices: Yaesu FT-991A, Icom IC-9700, HB9 repeater network
modulation: FM, SSB, CW, DMR, D-STAR, C4FM
power_limit: Varies by license class (typically 50 W for HB3, higher for HB9)
regulatory_ref: BAKOM (OFCOM Switzerland) national frequency allocation plan; Swiss RRL (Radio and Telecommunications Regulation)
notes: In Switzerland, 433.05-434.79 MHz is designated as ISM band - amateur stations must accept interference from ISM applications. Fixed service allocated on primary basis across 430-440 MHz per ITU footnote. Bands 430-435 MHz and 438-440 MHz also allocated to mobile (except aeronautical mobile) on primary basis.

application: Limited amateur radio allocation. Government/military has primary use. LPD433 license-free band overlays at 433.075-434.775 MHz.
typical_devices: Baofeng UV-5R (popular imported handheld), Yaesu FT-60R, various Russian-made equipment
regulatory_ref: GRFC frequency allocation; Russian Federation amateur radio regulations
notes: Russia has limited amateur allocation in 430-440 MHz. In practice, high power operation is common on LPD433 frequencies (433.075-434.775 MHz) despite regulations. Russian operators also commonly use LPD and PMR446 frequencies for cross-band CB repeater links. Amateur radio licensing in Russia managed by GRFC.

application: Limited amateur radio in some provinces. Government/military primary.
typical_devices: Baofeng UV-5R, TYT MD-UV380 (popular Chinese-made DMR handheld), various locally manufactured equipment
regulatory_ref: MIIT frequency allocation table; CRAC (Chinese Radio Amateur Club) regulations
notes: China's amateur allocation at 430-440 MHz is limited and varies by province. SRRC type approval required for all radio equipment. Amateur licensing managed by CRAC under MIIT supervision. Some provinces have additional restrictions. ISM-like use at 433 MHz is not formally designated as in Region 1.

application: License-free short range devices: home automation, weather stations, car key fobs, TPMS sensors, wireless doorbells, garage door openers, alarm systems, remote controls, IoT sensors, LoRa devices.
typical_devices: Somfy RTS blinds/shutters (433.42 MHz, OOK+Manchester, rolling code), Renault/PSA car key fobs (433.92 MHz), Netatmo weather station, Chacon/DIO 433.92 MHz home automation modules, RFXCOM RFXtrx433E transceiver (433.92 MHz + 433.42 MHz Somfy TX), Friedland wireless doorbells (433.92 MHz)
modulation: OOK (On-Off Keying), ASK, FSK, GFSK, LoRa (CSS)
power_limit: 10 mW ERP (with 10% duty cycle) or 1 mW ERP (no duty cycle limit for some applications)
regulatory_ref: ETSI EN 300 220; ERC/REC 70-03 Annex 1; ANFR SRD table; EU Decision 2006/771/EC (as amended)
notes: CRITICAL EUROPEAN SRD BAND. Sub-bands: (1) 433.05-434.79 MHz at 10 mW ERP with <=10% duty cycle for non-specific SRDs; (2) 433.05-434.79 MHz at 1 mW ERP with advanced mitigation for voice; (3) 434.04-434.79 MHz at 10 mW ERP with NO duty cycle limit, 25 kHz max channel spacing. This band is ISM only in ITU Region 1 (Europe/Africa/Middle East). France additionally restricts some sub-bands where military/defense systems operate (per ECC Rec 70-03 notes on h2/h3 sub-bands).

application: License-free short range devices: home automation, weather stations, car key fobs, TPMS sensors, wireless doorbells, garage door openers, alarm systems, IoT sensors.
typical_devices: VW/BMW/Mercedes car key fobs (433.92 MHz), Hormann garage door openers (433.92 MHz, rolling code; newer models use BiSecur 868.3 MHz), Oregon Scientific weather stations (433.92 MHz), ELV/Homematic 433 MHz devices, Somfy RTS (433.42 MHz)
power_limit: 10 mW ERP (10% duty cycle) or 1 mW ERP (voice with APC/AFA)
regulatory_ref: ETSI EN 300 220; ERC/REC 70-03 Annex 1; BNetzA Allgemeinzuteilung Vfg Nr. 40/2020
notes: Germany designates 433.05-434.79 MHz (centre 433.92 MHz) as ISM band per ITU RR footnote 5.138. Amateur radio services operating in this band must accept harmful interference from ISM applications. Sub-band 434.04-434.79 MHz allows 10 mW ERP without duty cycle restriction at 25 kHz spacing. BNetzA general allocation (Allgemeinzuteilung) covers non-specific SRDs.

application: License-free short range devices. Exempt from individual licensing under Ofcom IR 2030.
typical_devices: Byron wireless doorbells (433.92 MHz), car key fobs (433.92 MHz), CAME/NICE garage door openers (433.92 MHz), Oregon Scientific weather sensors (433.92 MHz), Yale alarm system sensors, LoRa IoT nodes
regulatory_ref: Ofcom IR 2030 (UK Interface Requirements 2030); ETSI EN 300 220; UK Radio Equipment Regulations 2017
notes: UK maintains alignment with European SRD framework post-Brexit through IR 2030. Same technical parameters as EU. Overlays amateur 70cm band (430-440 MHz) where amateur is secondary. 434.04-434.79 MHz sub-band allows 10 mW ERP without duty cycle limit at 25 kHz max occupied bandwidth.

application: License-free short range devices per EU harmonized framework.
typical_devices: Car key fobs (433.92 MHz), weather stations, garage door openers, home automation, alarm sensors
regulatory_ref: ETSI EN 300 220; ERC/REC 70-03 Annex 1; CNAF; Spanish Royal Decree on SRD
notes: Spain follows EU harmonized SRD framework. Sub-bands h2 and h3 may be limited in Spain where defense/governmental systems operate. Standard 433.92 MHz devices widely used.

application: License-free short range devices per EU harmonized framework.
typical_devices: Car key fobs (433.92 MHz, Fiat/Alfa Romeo/Lancia), CAME gate openers (433.92 MHz), NICE gate openers (433.92 MHz), weather stations, alarm sensors
regulatory_ref: ETSI EN 300 220; ERC/REC 70-03 Annex 1; MIMIT (formerly MISE) frequency plan
notes: Italy follows EU harmonized SRD framework. Notable that this ISM band overlaps with the amateur band gap at 434-435 MHz (where amateurs cannot operate in Italy). CAME and NICE are Italian manufacturers of gate/garage automation widely using 433.92 MHz.

application: License-free short range devices. Switzerland follows CEPT/ETSI framework despite not being EU member.
typical_devices: Car key fobs (433.92 MHz), weather stations, garage door openers, alarm sensors, Somfy RTS (433.42 MHz)
regulatory_ref: ETSI EN 300 220; ERC/REC 70-03 Annex 1; BAKOM/OFCOM Switzerland national allocation plan
notes: Switzerland specifically listed in ITU RR footnote 5.138 designating 433.05-434.79 MHz as ISM. BAKOM applies same SRD parameters as EU. Amateur radio services must accept harmful interference from ISM applications in this band.

application: Very limited unlicensed operation under FCC Part 15.231. Restricted to periodic transmitters: remote controls, security alarms, sensor reporting. NOT an ISM band in the US (US ISM is 902-928 MHz).
typical_devices: Some imported 433 MHz garage door remotes, tire pressure sensors (though US mainly uses 315 MHz for TPMS/RKE), wireless weather sensor receivers (limited)
power_limit: Field strength limit: ~11.8 mV/m at 3 meters (approximately -1.4 dBm / 0.72 mW for a quarter-wave antenna); max bandwidth 0.25% of center frequency
regulatory_ref: FCC 47 CFR Part 15.231 (Periodic operation above 70 MHz); Part 15.209 (general emission limits)
notes: CRITICAL DIFFERENCE: The US does NOT have an ISM band at 433 MHz. FCC Part 15.231 allows only periodic (non-continuous) operation for remote controls and alarms. Manually operated transmitters must deactivate within 5 seconds of release. Polling/supervision transmissions limited to 2 seconds per hour per transmitter. The US equivalent ISM band is 902-928 MHz. Most US car key fobs use 315 MHz, not 433.92 MHz. European 433 MHz devices are generally NOT FCC-compliant for US use.

application: License-free low power devices and walkie-talkies. Russia's alternative to European PMR446. 69 channels for narrow FM voice and data.
typical_devices: Baofeng BF-888S (commonly used on LPD frequencies), Motorola TLKR T50, various Chinese-manufactured LPD radios, Midland G5
modulation: NFM (Narrowband FM) for voice, OOK/FSK for data devices
power_limit: 10 mW ERP (official limit, though widely exceeded in practice)
regulatory_ref: Russian Federation radio regulation; GRFC general authorization for LPD433
notes: 69 channels starting at 433.075 MHz, ending at 434.775 MHz, spaced 25 kHz apart. In practice, Russian operators commonly exceed the 10 mW power limit. LPD433 and PMR446 frequencies are also used for cross-band CB repeater links in Russia and former Soviet countries. High power use is common despite regulations. LPD433 is Russia's primary license-free personal communications allocation (rather than PMR446 which is European).

application: Somfy RTS (Radio Technology Somfy) motorized blinds, shutters, awnings, and screen control. Dominant home automation protocol in France for window coverings.
typical_devices: Somfy Telis 1/4 RTS remote, Somfy Smoove Origin RTS wall switch, Somfy Situo 5 RTS, Somfy Connexoon RTS gateway, RFXCOM RFXtrx433E (433.42 MHz Somfy TX + 433.92 MHz general TX)
modulation: OOK (On-Off Keying) with Manchester encoding. Bit period ~604 us. Frame: preamble (hardware sync pulses + software sync) followed by 56 bits (7 bytes) of scrambled data.
regulatory_ref: ETSI EN 300 220; Somfy proprietary protocol (reverse-engineered: pushstack.wordpress.com/somfy-rts-protocol/)
notes: Somfy uses EXACTLY 433.42 MHz (NOT 433.92 MHz) for the RTS protocol. Data is Manchester encoded: rising edge = 1, falling edge = 0. 56-bit payload scrambled by XORing each byte with previous scrambled byte. Rolling code is 16 bits wide but receiver acceptance window of ~100 codes means effective entropy is 9-10 bits. Frame structure: wake-up pulses, hardware sync (2 high pulses), software sync (1 long high pulse of ~4550 us), then Manchester-encoded data. Somfy has shipped over 200 million RTS devices worldwide.

service: SRD - European TPMS, RKE, Weather Stations, Home Automation
application: Primary frequency for European automotive TPMS (Tire Pressure Monitoring System), RKE (Remote Keyless Entry), wireless weather stations, home automation, wireless doorbells, garage door openers.
typical_devices: Renault/PSA/VW/BMW/Mercedes car key fobs (433.92 MHz RKE with rolling code), European TPMS sensors (433.92 MHz, NOT 315 MHz), Oregon Scientific weather stations (433.92 MHz OOK protocol), Chacon/DIO 433.92 MHz switches, Friedland/Byron doorbells (433.92 MHz)
modulation: OOK, ASK, FSK (varies by device type and manufacturer)
regulatory_ref: ETSI EN 300 220; EU Directive 2006/771/EC; UNECE Regulation 141 (TPMS mandate EU 2014+)
notes: 433.92 MHz is the CENTER FREQUENCY of the European ISM/SRD band. European cars use 433.92 MHz for BOTH TPMS and key fobs (NOT 315 MHz which is the US/Japan frequency). This is a critical regional difference. TPMS mandatory in EU since November 1, 2012 (new type approvals) / November 1, 2014 (all new vehicles) for new cars. Oregon Scientific RF protocols (v1.0, v2.1, v3.0) all use 433.92 MHz OOK modulation. Hormann older garage openers use 433.92 MHz (newer BiSecur system uses 868.3 MHz). CAME and NICE Italian gate openers also use 433.92 MHz.

service: SRD - TPMS, RKE, Weather Stations, Home Automation
application: European automotive TPMS, RKE, wireless sensors, home automation, garage door openers.
typical_devices: VW/BMW/Mercedes/Audi car key fobs (433.92 MHz), European TPMS sensors, Hormann HSE 2 garage opener (433.92 MHz, rolling code), ELV weather sensors, Homematic 433 MHz sensors
regulatory_ref: ETSI EN 300 220; BNetzA Allgemeinzuteilung
notes: German automotive manufacturers (VW Group, BMW, Mercedes-Benz) all use 433.92 MHz for European-market key fobs and TPMS. Hormann (German garage door manufacturer) offers both 433.92 MHz (legacy HSM4/HSE2) and 868.3 MHz (BiSecur, from 2005+) systems.

application: UHF business band (Part 90), amateur radio upper 70cm (Part 97 up to 450 MHz), public safety, industrial.
typical_devices: Motorola APX 8000 (public safety P25), Kenwood NX-5300 (NXDN/DMR), amateur repeaters (typically 440-450 MHz output, 445-450 input with +5 MHz offset)
power_limit: Amateur: 1500 W PEP; Part 90: varies by license (typically 2-50 W mobile)
regulatory_ref: FCC 47 CFR Part 90 (land mobile); Part 97 (amateur, 420-450 MHz)
notes: US amateur band extends to 450 MHz (not 440 as in Region 1). 440-450 MHz is shared between amateur radio (secondary above 440 MHz in some areas) and land mobile services. Part 90 UHF business band frequencies are individually licensed. 12.5 kHz narrowband mandate applies to Part 90 operations.

application: Professional mobile radio (PMR), fixed links, government/military.
typical_devices: Motorola DP4800 (DMR, 403-470 MHz), Hytera PD685 (DMR), Kenwood NX-3320 (NXDN/DMR)
power_limit: Varies by license (typically up to 25 W mobile)
regulatory_ref: ANFR TNRBF; ARCEP frequency authorization
notes: 440-450 MHz in France allocated to fixed and mobile services. Professional mobile radio users require ARCEP frequency authorization. Some sub-bands used by military.

application: Professional mobile radio, Programme Making and Special Events (PMSE), some government use.
typical_devices: Motorola DP4800, Hytera PD685, PMSE talkback systems
regulatory_ref: Ofcom UKFAT; Ofcom Business Radio license terms
notes: Transition band between amateur (430-440 MHz) and major PMSE/PMR usage (450-470 MHz). Some 440-450 MHz used for business radio and PMSE applications.

application: Professional mobile radio, government communications, utilities.
typical_devices: Motorola DP4800, Hytera PD785, Kenwood NX-3320
regulatory_ref: BNetzA Frequenzplan
notes: 440-450 MHz allocated to fixed and mobile services in Germany. Licensed PMR operations.

application: License-free analog FM walkie-talkies for personal and business use. No license, no fee, no registration required.
typical_devices: Motorola Talkabout T82 Extreme (500 mW, 8/16 ch, IPx4, 800 mAh NiMH), Motorola Talkabout T62 (500 mW, 16 ch), Midland G9 Pro (PMR446, 8/16 ch, waterproof), Cobra AM1035 FLT
regulatory_ref: ECC Decision (15)05; ETSI EN 300 296-2; EU Decision 2018/1538
notes: 16 analog channels from 446.00625 to 446.19375 MHz at 12.5 kHz spacing. Originally 8 channels (Ch1-8: 446.00625-446.09375), expanded to 16 in 2018 by extending analog into the former digital-only 446.1-446.2 MHz segment. Integral (non-removable) antenna mandatory. Maximum 500 mW ERP. External antennas and repeaters prohibited for PMR446. Channel 1: 446.00625 MHz, Channel 2: 446.01875 MHz, etc.

application: License-free digital walkie-talkies using dPMR (FDMA) technology. Better spectral efficiency than analog with 6.25 kHz channels.
typical_devices: Kenwood TK-3601D/TK-3601DE (dPMR446+PMR446, 48 total channels: 32 digital + 16 analog, IP67, MIL-STD, Li-Ion 2200 mAh, up to 19 hrs operation)
regulatory_ref: ECC Decision (15)05; ETSI EN 300 113-2; ETSI EN 301 166-2; ETSI EN 303 405
notes: 32 digital dPMR channels from 446.003125 to 446.196875 MHz at 6.25 kHz spacing. dPMR uses FDMA to split each 12.5 kHz FM channel into two 6.25 kHz digital channels, doubling capacity vs analog. Extended to full 446.0-446.2 MHz band from 2018 per ECC Decision (15)05. dPMR Association manages standards compliance.

application: License-free digital walkie-talkies using DMR Tier 1 (TDMA) technology. Two timeslots per 12.5 kHz channel.
typical_devices: Motorola TLK-110 (DMR Tier 1 PMR446), Hytera PD365 (DMR PMR446), Retevis RT68
modulation: 4-level FSK (4FSK) at 3.6 kbit/s, TDMA (2 timeslots per 12.5 kHz channel)
regulatory_ref: ECC Decision (15)05; ETSI EN 300 113-2; ETSI EN 303 405
notes: 16 channels using DMR Tier 1 TDMA with 12.5 kHz spacing (same channel plan as analog). Each channel provides 2 timeslots, effectively 32 talk paths. From 2018, digital DMR extended onto 446.0-446.1 MHz (previously analog-only). DMR and dPMR are incompatible digital modes.

application: License-free walkie-talkies per EU harmonization.
typical_devices: Motorola Talkabout T82, Midland G9 Pro, Kenwood TK-3601DE, Albrecht Tectalk Float
modulation: NFM analog (12.5 kHz), dPMR FDMA (6.25 kHz), DMR TDMA (12.5 kHz)
regulatory_ref: ECC Decision (15)05; BNetzA Allgemeinzuteilung; ETSI EN 300 296-2; ETSI EN 303 405
notes: Same parameters as all CEPT countries. BNetzA implements via general allocation (Allgemeinzuteilung). No license required. Integral antenna mandatory.

application: License-free walkie-talkies. Widely used for personal, business, events, outdoor activities.
typical_devices: Motorola Talkabout T82, Midland G9 Pro, Kenwood TK-3601DE, Binatone Action 1100
modulation: NFM analog (12.5 kHz), dPMR FDMA (6.25 kHz), DMR TDMA (12.5 kHz)
regulatory_ref: Ofcom IR 2030; ECC Decision (15)05; UK Wireless Telegraphy (Licence Exemption) Regulations
notes: UK maintains PMR446 post-Brexit under Ofcom IR 2030. Same technical parameters as EU. Integral antenna mandatory. No external antennas or repeaters.

application: License-free walkie-talkies per EU harmonization.
typical_devices: Motorola Talkabout T82, Midland G9 Pro, Kenwood TK-3601DE
regulatory_ref: ECC Decision (15)05; CNAF; Spanish telecommunications regulations
notes: Spain follows EU-harmonized PMR446 standard. No license required.

application: License-free walkie-talkies per EU harmonization.
typical_devices: Motorola Talkabout T82, Midland G9 Pro (Midland is Italian brand), Kenwood TK-3601DE
regulatory_ref: ECC Decision (15)05; MIMIT frequency plan; Italian telecommunications regulations
notes: Italy follows EU-harmonized PMR446 standard. Midland (C.T.E. International) is an Italian company and major PMR446 radio manufacturer. No license required.

application: License-free walkie-talkies. Switzerland adopts CEPT PMR446 framework.
typical_devices: Motorola Talkabout T82, Midland G9 Pro, Kenwood TK-3601DE
regulatory_ref: ECC Decision (15)05; BAKOM/OFCOM Switzerland regulations
notes: Switzerland (non-EU but CEPT member) implements PMR446 under BAKOM regulations, aligned with ECC Decision (15)05. No license required.

service: NOT AVAILABLE - PMR446 does not exist in US
application: PMR446 is NOT used in the United States. The US equivalent is FRS (Family Radio Service) on 462/467 MHz.
typical_devices: N/A for PMR446. US equivalent: Motorola Talkabout T800/T600 (FRS, 462/467 MHz, 2W on FRS channels), Midland X-TALKER T71VP3
regulatory_ref: FCC 47 CFR Part 95 Subpart B (FRS); NOT PMR446
notes: PMR446 (446.0-446.2 MHz) is a EUROPEAN standard. The US uses FRS (Family Radio Service) at 462.5625-467.7125 MHz (22 channels, up to 2W ERP). Using PMR446 radios in the US would violate FCC regulations. Frequencies around 446 MHz in the US are allocated to land mobile and amateur radio services.

application: PMR446 has limited use in Russia. LPD433 (433.075-434.775 MHz) is the more commonly used license-free band.
typical_devices: Some imported PMR446 radios (Motorola, Midland), though LPD433 radios more common
regulatory_ref: GRFC regulations
notes: Russia primarily uses LPD433 (433.075-434.775 MHz, 69 channels, 10 mW) as their license-free alternative. PMR446 has some adoption but LPD433 is traditional. In practice, operators often exceed power limits on both bands. Cross-band repeater linking between LPD/PMR446, VHF, and 11m CB is common in Russia.

application: China does NOT have a PMR446 equivalent. License-free radio limited to specific MIIT-approved bands and devices.
typical_devices: N/A for PMR446. China uses public network walkie-talkie apps (Zello-like) and some MIIT-approved UHF devices on different frequencies.
regulatory_ref: MIIT radio regulations; SRRC type approval requirements
notes: China has no direct equivalent to PMR446 or FRS. All radio transmitting equipment requires SRRC type approval. License-free personal radio communications are very restricted compared to Europe and North America. Some consumer walkie-talkies operate on MIIT-approved frequencies in the 400-470 MHz range but require specific type approval.

application: Professional mobile radio (PMR), PAMR (trunked), SNCF railway, utility company communications, some government use.
typical_devices: Motorola DP4800 (DMR, 403-470 MHz), Hytera PD785, SNCF train radio equipment, utility SCADA systems
power_limit: Up to 25 W mobile, 50 W base station (licensed)
regulatory_ref: ANFR TNRBF; ARCEP authorization
notes: In France, 450-460/460-470 MHz includes SNCF railway radio allocations, utility company networks (EDF, Engie), and PMR. SNCF transitioning to GSM-R/FRMCS but legacy 450 MHz systems remain on some lines. ARCEP manages commercial PMR licensing.

application: Professional mobile radio, LTE 450 MHz (Band 72) for critical infrastructure, smart grid, smart metering.
typical_devices: 450 Connect LTE network equipment (Band 72, smart grid/metering), Motorola DP4800 (DMR PMR), Sierra Wireless HL7845 (LTE-M 450 MHz module for smart meters), Westermo cellular routers
modulation: LTE (OFDMA/SC-FDMA for Band 72), FM analog, DMR
power_limit: LTE Band 72: 23 dBm UE; PMR: varies by license
regulatory_ref: BNetzA Frequenzplan; 450 Connect license (Band 72); 3GPP Band 72 specifications
notes: NOTABLE: Germany has deployed LTE 450 MHz (3GPP Band 72) via 450 Connect for critical infrastructure. The network supports smart meters, smart grids, substation automation, and emergency voice communications. 450 MHz LTE provides superior building penetration compared to higher frequencies. The 450 Alliance promotes worldwide adoption. Band 72 is FDD: 451-456 MHz (uplink) / 461-466 MHz (downlink).

application: Professional mobile radio, PMSE (Programme Making and Special Events), business radio, utility networks.
typical_devices: Motorola DP4800 (DMR), Hytera PD685, PMSE talkback equipment, Icom IC-F4262DT
regulatory_ref: Ofcom UKFAT; Ofcom Business Radio license; IR 2030
notes: The 450-470 MHz band (UHF-2) is the MOST utilized PMSE band in the UK, with over 47,000 PMSE assignment allocations in 2022 (representing ~70% of all PMSE assignments). Includes extensive business radio, talkback systems for broadcast and events, and some utility applications. Ofcom has explored whether this band could support utility smart grid networks.

application: UHF business band (Part 90), public safety, industrial, transportation. One of the most heavily used land mobile bands in the US.
typical_devices: Motorola APX 8000 (P25 Phase II), Kenwood NX-5300 (NXDN/DMR/P25), Harris XL-200P (P25), Icom IC-F7010T
modulation: FM analog (legacy), P25 Phase I (C4FM FDMA), P25 Phase II (H-DQPSK TDMA), DMR, NXDN
power_limit: 2-50 W (varies by license class and equipment)
regulatory_ref: FCC 47 CFR Part 90; FCC narrowband mandate (12.5 kHz since 2013)
notes: UHF business band 450-470 MHz is individually licensed under Part 90. FCC narrowband mandate requires 12.5 kHz channel spacing (effective January 1, 2013, ending use of 25 kHz channels). Band split: 450-460 MHz (base transmit) / 460-470 MHz (mobile transmit) with 10 MHz offset for repeater operations. Heavily congested in urban areas. Public safety agencies transitioning to P25.

application: Professional mobile radio, government communications, some utility networks.
typical_devices: Motorola DP4800, Hytera PD785, Russian-manufactured radio equipment
regulatory_ref: GRFC frequency allocation; Russian telecommunications regulations
notes: 450-470 MHz in Russia used for government and commercial PMR. Some interest in LTE 450 MHz deployment for utilities and rural broadband, though implementation status varies by region.

application: Land mobile radio, professional communications, government use.
typical_devices: Hytera PD780 (DMR, Chinese manufacturer), Motorola DP4800, various Chinese-manufactured DMR/analog radios
regulatory_ref: MIIT frequency allocation table; SRRC type approval
notes: China's 450-470 MHz allocated to land mobile services. All equipment requires SRRC type approval. Hytera (Shenzhen) is a major Chinese manufacturer of DMR radios operating in this band. Some consideration of LTE 450 MHz for rural broadband.

application: Professional mobile radio, government communications, utilities.
typical_devices: Motorola DP4800, Hytera PD785, Kenwood NX-3320
regulatory_ref: CNAF; Spanish Ministry of Digital Transformation
notes: Spain allocates 450-470 MHz for fixed and mobile services. TETRA networks for emergency services (SIRDEE) operate in some portions. Licensed PMR users managed by Spanish telecommunications authority. [FACTCHECK CORRECTION: SIRDEE TETRA operates at 380-400 MHz, not 450-470 MHz. This band hosts other Spanish PMR/PAMR services.]

application: Professional mobile radio, government communications, utilities, railway.
typical_devices: Motorola DP4800, Hytera PD785, Kenwood NX-3320
regulatory_ref: MIMIT (formerly MISE) frequency plan; Italian telecommunications regulations
notes: Italy allocates 450-470 MHz for fixed and mobile services. Includes licensed PMR for utilities, transport, and industrial users. TETRA for some public safety applications.

application: Professional mobile radio, government communications, railway, utilities.
typical_devices: Motorola DP4800, Hytera PD785
regulatory_ref: BAKOM/OFCOM Switzerland national allocation plan
notes: Switzerland allocates 450-470 MHz for fixed and mobile services. BAKOM manages licensing. Swiss public safety uses Polycom TETRA network (primarily 380-400 MHz but with some 450 MHz infrastructure). [FACTCHECK CORRECTION: Swiss Polycom TETRAPOL operates at 380-400 MHz, not 450 MHz.]
